title: Maximizing the Power of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72: NVLink Domain-Aware Placement Groups in Ray
gist: Anyscale is adding NVLink Domain-Aware Placement Groups to Ray so scheduling units match NVIDIA GB200/GB300 NVL72 racks (72 Blackwell GPUs, 36 Grace CPUs, 1,800 GB/s all-to-all per GPU) rather than 8-GPU nodes. NVIDIA's GEAR lab measured 1.13x faster training iterations on a 512-GPU VLA pre-training run purely from rack-aware actor placement, plus rack-preserving fault recovery — evidence that on rack-scale hardware a meaningful slice of delivered FLOPs is now unlocked by orchestration software, not silicon.

themes.theme: Rack replaces node as the compute unit

insights.claim: NVIDIA GB200 NVL72 and GB300 NVL72 connect a full rack of 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs at 1,800 GB/s of all-to-all bandwidth per GPU, so the whole rack behaves as a single accelerator rather than as a network of servers.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: The purchasing and scheduling unit for frontier AI shifts from the 8-GPU server to the rack, which reshapes datacenter design, power density and how cloud capacity is sold.
insights.quote: connecting a full rack of 72 Blackwell GPUs and 36 Grace CPUs with 1,800 GB/s of all-to-all bandwidth per GPU, effectively enabling all GPUs to work together as one
insights.locator: Multi-Node NVLink Scale-up: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72

insights.claim: The prior generation topology — DGX H100/H200 packing 8 GPUs per node over NVLink/SXM and using InfiniBand or RoCE between nodes — is explicitly framed as the baseline that rack-scale NVLink displaces for communication-bound workloads.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Watch demand mix shift from scale-out fabrics (InfiniBand/RoCE ports per GPU) toward scale-up NVLink content as NVL72-class racks proliferate.
insights.quote: Traditional GPU servers like the NVIDIA DGX H100 and DGX H200 pack 8 GPUs into a single node connected by NVLink over SXM, with communication between nodes generally using InfiniBand or RoCE.
insights.locator: Multi-Node NVLink Scale-up: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72

insights.claim: The advantage of GB200/GB300 NVL72 is claimed only for workloads where collective communication and memory transfer dominate, not for compute-bound work generally.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: A workload-dependent moat: buyers running embarrassingly parallel inference gain less from NVL72 pricing premiums than buyers running large-collective training or disaggregated serving.
insights.quote: For workloads where collective communications and memory transfer dominate, the GB200 and GB300 NVL72 are industry leading.
insights.locator: Multi-Node NVLink Scale-up: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72

insights.claim: Ray placement groups historically reasoned only about accelerator type per individual node (e.g. Hopper vs Blackwell) and had no notion of cross-node dependencies, meaning the scheduler could not express the topology that NVL72 hardware exposes.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Confirms an orchestration gap between shipped rack-scale hardware and the software that schedules it — a window where scheduler vendors capture value and where deployed GPU fleets underperform spec.
insights.quote: Previously Ray placement groups did not understand cross-node dependencies.
insights.locator: Introducing Ray NVLink Domain-Aware Placement Groups

insights.claim: Before this feature, requesting STRICT_PACK of 18 bundles of 4 GPUs and 2 CPUs each would simply fail to schedule because Ray interpreted it as a demand for one 72-GPU node, a concrete illustration that node-level packing semantics break at rack scale.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Buyers of NVL72 capacity should audit whether their scheduler can even express rack-local groups before assuming they will realize the advertised interconnect benefit.
insights.quote: it would not be scheduled because you would actually be requesting a single node which has 72 GPUs!
insights.locator: For example, if you tried to STRICT_PACK

insights.claim: The existing workaround — tagging each rack with a custom label such as ray.io/gpu-domain=rack-7 and pinning bundles with bundle_label_selector — is manual and composes badly with autoscaling and fault tolerance, so operators were trading elasticity for locality.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Manual rack pinning implies stranded capacity and lower effective utilization in current GB300 fleets — a hidden cost line that topology-aware schedulers can recover.
insights.quote: This is manual and it doesn’t compose well with autoscaling or fault-tolerance.
insights.locator: The previous workaround was to assign

insights.claim: The new interface is a declarative topology_strategy map on the placement group API, e.g. {ray.io/node-id: "PACK", ray.io/gpu-domain: "STRICT_PACK"}, which makes hardware topology a first-class, portable scheduling constraint instead of site-specific labels.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: A portable topology abstraction lets the same training code move between clouds and rack generations, strengthening Ray/Anyscale as the neutral layer above heterogeneous GPU estates.
insights.quote: topology_strategy = {ray.io/node-id: "PACK", ray.io/gpu-domain: "STRICT_PACK"}
insights.locator: To address this, we’re introducing NVLink Domain awareness

themes.theme: Measured payoff: NVIDIA GEAR VLA run

insights.claim: In a controlled A/B on NVIDIA GEAR's Vision Language Action pre-training, the topology-aware run achieved 1.13x faster iterations per second than the identical run without domain-aware placement — a ~13% throughput gain from scheduling alone, with no hardware change.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Roughly 13% of training throughput on rack-scale GPUs is a software line item, not a silicon one — that is real dollars per GPU-hour and a moat for orchestration layers.
insights.quote: The second run achieved 1.13x faster iterations per second than the first.
insights.locator: Real World Example: Large Scale Distributed VLA training on GB300

insights.claim: The benchmark ran at a credible production scale — 512 GPUs across 128 nodes, structured as 8 groups of 64 GPUs (16 nodes each) — rather than a toy cluster.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Scale of the test makes the 1.13x figure usable as a planning assumption for GB300 fleet ROI models, though it is vendor-run and single-workload.
insights.quote: Each run used 512 GPUs (128 nodes), composed of 8 groups of 64 GPUs (16 nodes).
insights.locator: Real World Example: Large Scale Distributed VLA training on GB300

insights.claim: The mechanism behind the speedup is that badly placed actors spend more time exchanging data with placement-group peers during collectives like all_reduce, whereas rack-local actors use NVLink GPU-to-GPU memory sharing — locating the bottleneck in communication, not compute.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Communication-bound training means interconnect locality, not FLOPs, is the marginal constraint — favoring vendors selling scale-up fabric and software that exploits it.
insights.quote: In run one, GPUs spend more time exchanging data with their placement group peers (for example during collective operations like all_reduce).
insights.locator: Why is the performance better in run two?

insights.claim: Anyscale explicitly frames the 1.13x as a floor rather than a ceiling, saying further opportunities remain to exploit GB300 hardware capabilities more effectively.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Expect successive software-only performance uplifts on already-installed GB300 racks, which raises effective capacity without new capex and can soften near-term GPU demand per unit of output.
insights.quote: However, this is just the beginning, as further opportunities remain to make even more effective use of the GB300’s unique hardware capabilities.
insights.locator: Real World Example: Large Scale Distributed VLA training on GB300

insights.claim: Domain-aware placement also unlocks NVIDIA SHARP in-network collective acceleration, meaning locality is a precondition for a second layer of communication optimization rather than a standalone gain.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Gains compound: schedulers that get locality right can then stack in-network acceleration, widening the gap versus topology-blind orchestrators.
insights.quote: it also allows us to take better advantage of new features to accelerate collective communications such as NVIDIA SHARP
insights.locator: Optimized networking performance

insights.claim: Ray now preserves topology intent through cluster churn: on node failure or maintenance it replaces the node from the same NVLink Domain when capacity exists, rather than silently fragmenting the job across racks and quietly degrading throughput.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Silent post-failure fragmentation is a plausible cause of unexplained throughput decay in long training runs — a diligence question for anyone underwriting GPU cluster efficiency claims.
insights.quote: Ray will replace the node from the same NVLink Domain when capacity exists rather than silently fragmenting the workload across racks.
insights.locator: Application-aware fault tolerance

insights.claim: When same-domain capacity is unavailable Ray queues the bundle for rescheduling, and only if the entire bundle set goes down does it automatically select a new NVLink Domain — an availability-versus-locality tradeoff that biases toward locality.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Operators need spare capacity headroom per rack (the GEAR run left 2 spares per domain) or jobs stall waiting for local slots — a utilization tax to model in cluster economics.
insights.quote: If capacity does not exist, the bundle is queued for rescheduling unless the entire set of bundles goes down where a new NVLink Domain is automatically selected for use.
insights.locator: Application-aware fault tolerance

themes.theme: Inference and RL as the wider market

insights.claim: Disaggregated inference that splits prefill and decode workers needs those workers inside the same NVLink Domain so KV cache and intermediate state travel the fastest path, making rack-aware scheduling an inference-serving requirement and not just a training optimization.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Inference is the larger and faster-growing spend pool; rack-scale locality requirements there extend NVL72-class hardware demand well beyond frontier training labs.
insights.quote: it is especially important that these workers land within the same NVLink Domain so they can exchange KV cache and intermediate state over the fastest available path
insights.locator: Other Use-cases for Rack-Aware Scheduling

insights.claim: Reinforcement learning pipelines have heterogeneous phases — training, rollout, evaluation — with different communication patterns, so the right model is selective colocation: pin weight-exchanging policy trainers to one domain while letting Ray scatter communication-light components.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Mixed-criticality placement means clusters can be provisioned with tiered interconnect rather than uniformly premium fabric, a cost lever for RL-heavy shops.
insights.quote: RL workloads have many phases: training, rollout, and evaluation, each with different communication patterns.
insights.locator: Other Use-cases for Rack-Aware Scheduling

insights.claim: The feature ships supporting only STRICT_PACK today, with STRICT_SPREAD (placing bundles on deliberately separate racks) still on the roadmap — so anti-affinity and blast-radius control are not yet expressible.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: V1 scope limits how far the reliability story goes today; incremental releases are the near-term catalyst for Ray/Anyscale adoption on rack-scale fleets.
insights.quote: NVLink Domain-Aware Placement Groups currently only support STRICT_PACK.
insights.locator: What's Next?

insights.claim: Anyscale states the topology model is flat today and plans nested topologies reflecting that racks sit inside datacenters inside availability zones, signaling a move toward hierarchy-aware scheduling across multi-rack and multi-region estates.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Hierarchical topology awareness is the precondition for efficient cross-datacenter training, the next scaling frontier once single-site power limits bind.
insights.quote: In reality, infrastructure is usually hierarchical where racks live within datacenters, which live within availability zones, and so on.
insights.locator: What's Next?

insights.claim: The stated primary goal is to raise NVLink Domain awareness into the Ray application layer, with more GPU-locality visibility and placement tooling promised over the next few releases — an admission that operators currently lack visibility into where their GPUs actually sit.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Observability of interconnect locality is an emerging product category; poor visibility today means reported cluster efficiency figures deserve scepticism.
insights.quote: we aim to provide even more visibility and tools to understand GPU locality and optimize placement for maximum performance and interconnect efficiency
insights.locator: What's Next?

insights.claim: Anyscale, the commercial steward of Ray, has signed a definitive agreement to join Nscale, per a linked item on the same page — placing the leading AI-workload orchestration layer inside a GPU cloud provider.
insights.speaker: Joshua Lee, Anyscale / Ray Blog
insights.so_what: Vertical integration of orchestration software into neocloud capacity is a consolidation signal; watch whether Ray topology features stay neutral across clouds or tilt toward Nscale hardware.
insights.quote: Anyscale signs definitive agreement to join Nscale
